messages.subject: RE: [gbm] More notes on coxph (#59)
parts:
Terry,

We generally use gbm...@googlegroups.com for our discussions, though I think I got your message through a post to the github site. Best to use the google groups.

GitHub we use a lot because now we have several people working on it and we need a way to handle feature requests and bug fixes, etc.

std::exp() to be explicit which exp() implementation to use... in this case drawing exp from the C++ standard library.

const assures that parameters going into the function are not changed by the function. This is good practice especially when there are a lot of people working on a project. When passing by reference, const communicates to the compiler that this object will not get changed so the compiler doesn't even think that it will need to make a copy of the object being passed in.

unsigned long... to be explicit about what kind of integer the function is expecting. However, I recognize that not all compilers have the same thoughts on how big a "long" should be. Eventually might think about defining our indexing integers with something like int8 so that throughout we know exactly the range of the integers used.

vecdRisktot[i] stores the total for case i's risk set. resize() is just a method for vector objects to allocate their length. Here coxph.cpp just makes sure that the vector is as long as the training dataset.

The type "bag" is defined in dataset.h as a vector of ints typedef std::vector<int> bag; Here I agree with you that this is confusing. I'd prefer to simply have std::vector<int> everywhere.
All of the variable names in the gbm package adopted conventional "hungarian" prefixes so that you can quickly see what type they are. So for afInbag the "a" means array and "f" means flag (true/false). So this is the array that tells the function which cases are bagged and which ones are not. Again the const is to make sure that the function does not change afInBag and the compiler knows that it does not need to prepare to make a copy of the array.

The CDistribution class in distribution.h has some of the documentation you need. All of the distributions, including CCoxPH, are subclasses of CDistribution and inherit its structure.

// In the subsequent functions, parameters have the following meaning:
// * adY - The target
// * adMisc - Optional auxiliary data (the precise meaning is specific to the
// derived class)
// * adOffset - An optional offset to the score (adF) // * adWeight - Instance training weight
// * adF - Current score (sum of all trees generated so far)
// * adZ - (Negative) gradient of loss function, to be predicted by tree
// * adFadj - Output of current tree, to be added to adF
// * cLength - Number of instances (size of vectors) // * afInBag - true if instance is part of training set for current tree
// (depends on random subsampling)
// * cIdxOff - Offset used for multi-class training (CMultinomial).

cIdxOff is probably going away in the next version. It got added in an attempt to implement the multinomial. The multinomial implementation was rather complicated and affected the design of the other distribution classes, so that recent efforts (heroic efforts by Metcalfe) have been removing the multinomial functionality to simplify the code.

The adMisc parameter is ignored by almost all the classes... possibly by all except CCoxPH. While the CDistribution class and all of the other classes tend to use adY and adMisc for these first two parameters, you will see in CCoxPH (in coxph.cpp) that they are named adT and adDelta, time and censoring indicators.

Lastly note that in gbm.fit.R that the observations are sorted up front from latest to earliest failure times so that in coxph.cpp it can compute risksets much faster. After the model is fit, then the predictions are put back in the original order. Just something to be aware of for the Cox model.

I'm happy to answer 20 more questions if it helps you get to the next stage. Basically, you should be thinking about writing functions for your new class: ComputeWorkingResponse, InitF, Deviance, FitBestConstant, and BagImprovement. If you can try to do that using coxph.cpp as a template, then either I or someone from the team can try it out, comment on it, propose ways to standardize it with the rest of gbm style/design. GitHub can facilitate this. You probably want to do a "fork & pull" (https://help.github.com/articles/using-pull-requests/). This lets you create your own gbm version, make changes, and then submit them to the team for testing.

Greg

Greg Ridgeway, Ph.D.
Associate Professor, Criminology and Statistics University of Pennsylvania

From: Therneau, Terry M., Ph.D. [mailto:ther...@mayo.edu]

To: Greg Ridgeway <gregri...@gmail.com>
Subject: Re: [gbm] More notes on coxph (#59)

Greg,
First I need a short tutorial on how to communicate with you folks. The text below came from "g...@noreply.githb.com", whis is not a very promising reply-to address. I expect it comes from some listserve type process that I am unfamiliar with. I created a github account and pulled a copy of gbm, but if you assume 0 github knowlege that is a good assumption. (I've just never needed it, and life it too crowded to learn things I don't yet need).

With respect to the note itself.

1. There are a lot of mysteries to the C++ code. (Why std::exp instead of exp? Why
"const double" for all the args? Why unsigned long? What is vecdRisktot.resize?) There
are no comments in coxph.cpp, so how is one to guess what the arguments are, and what to use them for --- cIdxOff? const bag & afInBag??? If you want to fill in the holes I can give it a shot, but right how it looks like a game of "20 questions".

Contributing validated C code is one thing, learning C++ is another and notrivial step. It almost certainly involves learning a new compile/test sequence.

2. As a statistician your gbm vignette is useful, though I knew much of that from the Hastie et al book. It says next to nothing about adding code.

3. You mention a "misc" parameter. No mention of this in coxph.cpp. There are a few references to something called misc_ptr in gbm.cpp, but not one of them has a comment.

The lack of program documentation makes this difficult terrain to traverse.

Terry T.


On 08/19/2015 11:48 AM, Greg Ridgeway wrote:
> The issue is less about C versus C++ but rather having the right gradient computations.
> Have a look at the vignette
>
> github.com/gbm-developers/gbm/blob/master/inst/doc/gbm.pdf
>
> If you have code for all of the necessary steps, then it is pretty
> easy to add a new distribution class to the package.
>
> Figure 2 shows the basic algorithm. The cox likelihood is more complex
> since it isn't a simple sum as shown in the figure, but the steps are
> basically the same. We need an initial value (0 is fine for Cox). We
> need the gradient d/df(x) Psi(t,delta,f(x)). We need the terminal node values.
>
> I would suggest starting with the coxph.cpp source. Copy it to
> coxphefron.cpp. Modify it so that it does Efron approximation. You
> might be able to reuse much of the code you already have. See if you can get that far. If so, then I think the rest will come easy.
>
> You can use the misc parameter in gbm.fit to pass extra parameters to the gbm engine.
>
> Greg
